questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: Raman’s friend’s tone was very
rude and sarcastic during the
entire duration of the meeting.
No Error
options_hi: Raman’s friend’s tone was very
rude and sarcastic during the
entire duration of the meeting.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (A).

Replace “Raman’s friend’s tone” with “The tone of Raman’s friend”.

Rule/Concept: Avoidance of Double Possessives -

In formal English grammar, the use of two consecutive nouns in the possessive case (Double Apostrophe) is considered grammatically incorrect. It creates structural clumsiness. To fix this, we use the "of" construction for the first possession and an apostrophe for the second, or vice versa, to ensure there is only one 's in a single phrase.

Application to the Given Question -

In this sentence, the possession is layered: the tone belongs to the friend, and the friend belongs to Raman. Using two apostrophes ("Raman's" and "friend's") back-to-back violates the rule of double possessives. By restructuring it to "The tone of Raman's friend," we maintain the relationship while adhering to standard grammatical norms.

Corrected Sentence - The tone of Raman’s friend was very rude and sarcastic during the entire duration of the meeting.

More Examples:-

Rohit’s brother’s car was stolen last night. ❌

The car of Rohit’s brother was stolen last night. ✅

Neha’s teacher’s advice helped me a lot. ❌

The advice of Neha’s teacher helped me a lot. ✅

questions.q_en:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.

Stop trying to __________ me by making fun of my presentation; it’s not funny anymore.
questions.q_hi:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.

Stop trying to __________ me by making fun of my presentation; it’s not funny anymore.
options_en: wind down
Wind up
Wind off
Wind out
options_hi: wind down
Wind up
Wind off
Wind out
questions.solution_en:
Explanation: The correct answer is option (2).

English Explanation: “Wind up” (informal usage) means to tease, irritate, or deliberately provoke someone, often in a playful way. In the sentence, the speaker is asking someone to stop making fun of their presentation, which shows irritation caused by teasing. Therefore, “wind up” correctly conveys the idea of provoking or irritating someone. “Wind down” means to relax or gradually come to an end. “Wind off” is not commonly used in this context and generally relates to removing something wound around an object. “Wind out” can mean to knock the breath out of someone but does not fit the idea of teasing. Since the context refers to irritating someone through teasing, “wind up” is the most appropriate fit.

1. Wind down (धीरे-धीरे शांत होना / समाप्त होना)
Meaning in Hindi: आराम करना या धीरे-धीरे किसी गतिविधि को समाप्त करना।
Example: After the meeting, we wound down with some light music. (बैठक के बाद हमने हल्का संगीत सुनकर आराम किया।)

2. Wind up (चिढ़ाना / परेशान करना; समाप्त करना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी को चिढ़ाना या किसी कार्य को समाप्त करना।
Example 1: His friends were just winding him up by joking about the exam results. (उसके दोस्त परीक्षा परिणामों पर मज़ाक करके उसे चिढ़ा रहे थे।)
Example 2: She wound up the discussion after two hours. (उसने दो घंटे बाद चर्चा समाप्त कर दी।)

3. Wind off (लपेट हटाना / निकालना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी चीज़ को लपेट से हटाना या निकालना।
Example: He wound off the tape from the old recorder. (उसने पुराने रिकॉर्डर से टेप निकाल लिया।)

4. Wind out (सांस निकाल देना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी की सांस निकाल देना या जोर से चोट लगना।
Example: The punch nearly winded him out. (घूंसे से उसकी लगभग सांस निकल गई।)

Rule / Concept: Avoid Double Negatives -

In English grammar, certain words carry a "negative" meaning on their own. When you use one of these words, you cannot use another negative word (like no, not, never, nothing, nobody) in the same clause. Doing so creates a "double negative," which technically cancels out the negation or, more commonly in exams, is simply considered ungrammatical.

Common "Hidden" Negatives:

Application to the Given Question - "She rarely approached nobody..."

Corrected Sentence - She rarely approached anybody to talk about the problems that she was facing.

questions.q_en: Little progress has been made despite repeated assurances from the authorities, ______?
questions.q_hi: Little progress has been made despite repeated assurances from the authorities, ______?
options_en: hasn’t it
has it
doesn’t it
did it
options_hi: hasn’t it
has it
doesn’t it
did it
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) - “has it”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Negative Meaning Word (“Little”) + Auxiliary Repetition

The word “little” (without “a”) carries a negative meaning (almost none).

When a statement is negative in meaning → the question tag must be positive.

Also, when the main clause contains an auxiliary verb (has/have/is/was etc.), we must repeat that auxiliary in the tag.

💢 Application to the Given Question

  • “Little progress” → negative meaning

  • Therefore → tag must be positive

  • The auxiliary used is has

  • Subject “progress” → replaced by it

So, the correct tag is: has it?

✅ More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅- Little improvement has occurred, has it?

Example 2 ✅ - Little attention was paid to the issue, was it?

Example 3 ✅ - Little effort has been shown so far, has it?

🧠 Things to Remember

  • “Little” (without “a”) = negative meaning.

  • Negative meaning → positive tag.

  • Repeat the same auxiliary from the main clause.

  • Do not get confused between “a little” (positive meaning) and “little” (negative meaning).

questions.q_en: If the central bank raises the cash reserve ratio in the upcoming review, liquidity in the market ____ sharply and borrowing costs ____ accordingly.
questions.q_hi: If the central bank raises the cash reserve ratio in the upcoming review, liquidity in the market ____ sharply and borrowing costs ____ accordingly.
options_en:
contracts / rises

will contract / will rise

would contract / would rise

had contracted / had risen
options_hi:
contracts / rises

will contract / will rise

would contract / would rise

had contracted / had risen
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

👉 Replace the blanks with “will contract / will rise”.

📌 Rule / Concept: First Conditional (Real Future Situation)

Structure: If + Present Simple, will + base verb

This structure is used for real and possible future situations. The condition is realistic, and the result is a likely future consequence.

💢 Application to the Given Sentence - If the central bank raises the cash reserve ratio in the upcoming review

This is a real future possibility (policy action).

Therefore, the result must show a real future effect:

✔ liquidity in the market will contract sharply
✔ borrowing costs will rise accordingly

We cannot use:

  • Present tense (contracts / rises) → because the situation refers to a specific future policy action.
  • Would → because this is not hypothetical or unreal.

✅ More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅- If inflation increases, interest rates will go up.

Example 2 ✅- If the government introduces stricter norms, compliance costs will rise.

Example 3 ✅- If the company fails to diversify, profits will decline.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: People in different parts of India
have their own distinct habits when
it comes to marriages and festivals.
No Error
options_hi: People in different parts of India
have their own distinct habits when
it comes to marriages and festivals.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “habits” with “customs”.

Rule / Concept: Habit vs. Custom

While both words refer to repeated actions, their application depends on the subject performing the action:

-Habit (Individual): Refers to a settled or regular tendency or practice, especially one that is hard to give up. It belongs to a single person.

Example: Smoking is a bad habit.

-Custom (Group/Society): Refers to a traditional and widely accepted way of behaving or doing something that is specific to a particular society, place, or time.

Example: It is a Japanese custom to bow when greeting.

Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the subject is "People in different parts of India" (a collective society or group). Marriages and festivals are not individual behavioral quirks; they are social traditions and rituals established by a culture. Therefore, the word "habits" is logically incorrect and should be replaced by "customs."

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1 - He has a habit of waking up at 5 AM every day. (Individual action)

Example 2 - The custom of dowry is considered a social evil. (Social practice)

Example 3 - Every country has its own unique customs and traditions.

questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: Most of the candidates have submitted their digital applications online
and so the remaining offline applicants have in accordance
with the updated guidelines provided in the official recruitment notification.
No Error
options_hi: Most of the candidates have submitted their digital applications online
and so the remaining offline applicants have in accordance
with the updated guidelines provided in the official recruitment notification.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “the remaining offline applicants have” with “have the remaining offline applicants”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Inversion after "So" in Affirmative Agreements

Positive statement :- SO+HV+SUB

When we want to avoid repeating a verb and express that a second subject has done the same thing as the first subject in an affirmative (positive) sentence, we use the structure: "So + Auxiliary Verb + Subject". This is a form of Partial Inversion where the auxiliary verb must precede the subject. The auxiliary verb must match the tense and aspect of the verb used in the first clause

💢 Application to the Given Question

...and so the remaining offline applicants have in accordance...

In the first part of the sentence, the auxiliary verb is "have" (Present Perfect). To show that the "remaining offline applicants" have also submitted their applications, we must use the inverted form after "so". Therefore, the auxiliary "have" must be placed before the subject "the remaining offline applicants".

Corrected Sentence

Most of the candidates have submitted their digital applications online and so have the remaining offline applicants in accordance with the updated guidelines provided in the official recruitment notification.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅: Rahul loves playing chess, and so does his younger brother.

Example 2 ✅: The manager was impressed with the results, and so were the directors.

Example 3 ✅: I have finished my homework, and so has my roommate.

Rule/Concept: Interrogative Modal "Dare/Need"- In the interrogative structure (especially with Wh-words like How, Who, Why), "Dare/Need" can function as a modal verb. When it acts as a modal in a question:

  1. It comes before the subject.

  2. It is followed by the Bare Infinitive (V1 without "to").

  3. It does not take 's' or 'es' regardless of whether the subject is singular or plural.

Things to Remember / Exam Tips

  1. The Missing 'Does': If the sentence were "How does the attorney dare to suggest...", it would be a main verb construction. If 'does' is missing, it's a modal construction—so skip the 's' and the 'to'.

  2. Wh-Trigger: "How dare..." is a classic SSC/Banking phrase. Always look for V1 immediately after the subject in such cases.

  3. Tense Check: While "dared" can be used for the past, in the modal form, "dare" is used for both present and past in many contexts, but "dares" is always wrong in a modal structure.

questions.q_en:
Modern societies often celebrate progress through visible indicators—economic growth, technological penetration, and expanding infrastructure—while quietly overlooking fractures that resist quantification. Social inequality, though frequently acknowledged in rhetoric, is often treated as an abstract concern rather than a lived reality. The persistence of unequal access to education, healthcare, and legal recourse reveals that disparity is not merely a residual flaw of development but, in many cases, its unintended companion. Progress, when unevenly distributed, can deepen the very divides it claims to bridge. Public discourse tends to individualize social failure. Poverty is reframed as lack of effort, marginalization as absence of adaptability, and exclusion as personal deficiency. Such narratives offer moral comfort to the privileged by converting structural disadvantage into personal responsibility. Over time, this framing dulls collective urgency. When inequality is perceived as self-inflicted, social empathy is replaced by conditional sympathy—extended only to those deemed “deserving.” Institutions, meanwhile, respond with procedural solutions that emphasize efficiency over equity. Welfare systems grow increasingly conditional, access mechanisms become more complex, and accountability is measured through compliance rather than outcome. While these approaches appear neutral, they disproportionately burden those already navigating scarcity. The result is a paradoxical system in which assistance exists formally but remains functionally inaccessible to many. The most corrosive consequence of persistent inequality is not material deprivation alone but the erosion of social trust. When large sections of society experience the state as distant or indifferent, civic engagement weakens and resentment quietly accumulates. Addressing social issues, therefore, requires more than policy expansion; it demands a recalibration of how societies assign blame, distribute dignity, and define progress itself.

“Such narratives offer moral comfort to the privileged by converting structural disadvantage into personal responsibility,”
the phrase “by converting structural disadvantage into personal responsibility” functions as:

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C).

Replace “flown” with “flowed”

📌 Rule/Concept: Confusing Pairs of Verbs (Fly vs. Flow) –

The error in this question stems from confusing two verbs that describe movement but apply to different subjects (air vs. liquid).

Fly – Flew – Flown: Used for birds, aircraft, or anything moving through the air.

Flow – Flowed – Flowed: Used for liquids (water, blood, oil, champagne) moving in a stream

The Trap: Examiners often use the form "flown" for liquids because it sounds like "flow," but "flown" is strictly for flying. Conversely, they might use "flowed" for birds

💢 Application to the Given Question -

In this sentence, the subject is champagne (a liquid). Since the champagne is moving out of a bottle (leaking or pouring), it is "flowing." The past participle (V3) required after the auxiliary "had" must be the V3 of Flow, which is flowed. Using "flown" implies the champagne grew wings and took flight into the sky.

More Examples for Clarity –

Example 1: The river flowed gently through the valley. (Liquid movement)

Example 2: The pilot has flown this route many times. (Air movement Example 3: Blood flowed from the wound. (Liquid movement)

had better to diversify their portfolios immediately.
No error

the financial consultant suggested that the investors

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “had better to diversify” with “had better diversify”

📌 Rule / Concept: The "Had Better" Construction

The phrase "Had better" is a semi-modal idiom used to give advice, express a preference, or issue a warning. Despite the presence of the word "had" (which looks like past tense) and "better" (which looks like a comparison), it functions as a single unit meaning "should" or "ought to."

The absolute rule for this idiom is that it must be followed by a Bare Infinitive (V1 without "to").

💢 Application to the Given Question

In lengthy, high-level questions, examiners surround the error with complex vocabulary like "volatile nature," "diversify," and "portfolios" to distract you from the simple verb pattern.

"...investors had better to diversify their portfolios..."

In the sentence above, the infinitive marker "to" has been incorrectly inserted before the verb "diversify." To correct the error, the "to" must be removed to satisfy the requirement of the bare infinitive.

Corrected Sentence "Given the volatile nature of the stock market this week, the financial consultant suggested that the investors had better diversify their portfolios immediately."

questions.solution_en:

Rule/Concept: Use of ‘THE’ before comparative degree when one of two is specified.

When a comparison is made between exactly two persons, things, or ideas, and one of them is shown to be superior, ‘THE’ must precede the comparative degree to convey a specific and definite sense.

Application to the Given Question - Here, the phrase “of the two explanations” clearly restricts the comparison to two only. Therefore, the accepted explanation must be identified as the more plausible one.

More Examples for Clarity –

1. Between the two routes, the shorter is preferred.
2. Of the two candidates, the more qualified was selected. 
3. Between the two answers, the better deserves full marks.

 

Things to Remember / Exam Tips –

Always look for phrases like between the two / of the two.
These phrases force the use of ‘the + comparative’. Absence of ‘the’ is a very common SSC trap. Never use comparative without ‘the’ when the choice is limited to two.

The captain said to the sailors, "If the wind stays strong, we will reach the shore by midnight."
options_en: The captain told the sailors that if the wind stays strong, they will reach the shore by midnight.
The captain told the sailors that if the wind stayed strong, they would reach the shore by midnight.
The captain told the sailors that if the wind had stayed strong, they would have reached the shore by midnight.
The captain told the sailors that if the wind stayed strong, we will reach the shore by midnight.

questions.solution_en:
The correct answer is Option B: The captain told the sailors that if the wind stayed strong, they would reach the shore by midnight.

Key Points

  • The Conditional Shift: the Simple Present ("stays") shifts to Simple Past ("stayed") because the reporting verb "said" is in the past.

  • Modal Conversion: The future "will" must be converted into "would" to maintain the sequence of tenses.

  • Reporting Verb: "said to" correctly changes to "told" because there is an object ("the sailors").

  • Pronoun Change: The first-person plural "we" changes to "they" because the captain is reporting the action of the group to someone else.

  • Eliminating Incorrect Options:

    • Option A is wrong because it fails to change the tense.

    • Option C is a "Type 3" conditional trap (Past Perfect); this is only used if the original direct speech was already in the past tense.

    • Option D is inconsistent because it changes the first verb but forgets to change "will" and the pronoun "we".
